en: Let no such excuse be found,
Let them not fall into needless trouble.
Let them not evade the order.
Let the wretched people witness this,
And not bring Judgment Day upon themselves.
Let no girl known
And recognized among the people be left out.
No girl due to leave for bridewealth,
No betrothed girl shall be left out!’
After Temir Khan had shown his wrath,
And the strongmen had heard the order,
They demanded girls from every household,
And gathered them, leaving none out.
Before the judges,
They drove them in.
Girls filed this way and that;
Bukhara was thrown into confusion.
When the fortress in Bukhara
Was crowded with swarming girls,
Koloy Khan of Bukhara,
Straight-hearted and plain-spoken,
An exceptional judge, clear-sighted—
That Koloy whom you have seen,
Who would break his bonds and die,
Loved the orphan son of Manas
With an exceptional love.
Never to spill from his palm,
He cherished him like gathered treasure.
As the warm life within his breast,
As his faith, he cherished him.
Bukhara's lord Koloy,
Taking a short way through the interior,
From among the filing girls
Brought out one girl,
Lord Koloy leading her by the hand.
The girl whom he led
Was the child of a noble family,
The daughter of Shaatemir.
She was still a young child,
Her hair not yet long enough to braid,
Her age not yet beyond fourteen.
On her head was a cap made of gold.
Shaatemir's Chachykei,
An extremely beautiful, bold girl,
Her waist a handspan, her face like the moon.
If blood should fall upon the dark earth,
Look at snow, then at her complexion.
If blood should fall upon the snow,
Look at that blood, then at her face.
Look at a pistachio, then at her teeth.
Look at the craftsmen's wire,
Look at that wire, then at her hair.
Look at an apple, then at her head.
The sight diverted one's heart;
Like the feathers of a parrot,
She appeared in many changing hues.
Koloy had judged and chosen her.
Cutting off a head when told to take a cap,
Temir Khan's strongman
To the khan's golden throne
Brought Shaatemir's daughter Chachykei,
Taking hold of her and leading her there.
Shaatemir of Bukhara,
Temir Khan and Koloy—these
Were the children of brothers.
Before Temir Khan,
Shaatemir went and made his plea:
‘To this orphan son of Manas,
I am glad you are giving her.
But Toltoy is her betrothed;
Trouble will arise afterward,
And that is why I grieve!
When the Zhediger in Zheti-Suu
Went forth in high spirits,
The hero of the Zhediger,
The accomplished Bagysh, was khan.
Beyond broad Kashgar,
Along great Sary-Kol,
The youngest of nine sons,
A servant of the one God,
The champion among many mighty men—
Eleman's hero Toshtuk—
Since he had gone beneath the earth,
Seven years had passed.
Since he had returned above the earth,
Forty-seven days had passed.
From Eleman's countless herds,
Nine hundred barren mares were slaughtered.
The people gathered for festivities,
And wise old Koshoi was there.
The precious warrior Manas was absent;
All the other mighty heroes were there:
Zhamgyrchy from the Eshteks,
Khan Kokcho from the Kazakhs,
Muzburchak, son of Buudaiyk—
Which of them shall we name?
The multitude, the people were there,
The heroes of every nation were there,
All the Muslim people were there then.
Skilled lancers were there,
And worthy men of full resource.
Just and worthy khans were there;
All the people were there.
The Zhediger's hero Bagysh,
Who is Toltoy's father—
All those men
Blessed the betrothal to Chachykei.
Driving livestock to seal the marriage bond,
At that feast of Toshtuk,
You bowed in thanks, chewing fat.
Driving six hundred piebald beasts,
Turning the hearts of those who saw,
A white-gray horse as large as a hut,
Upon that horse's forelock
A bowl-sized silk ornament was displayed.
‘May your marriage alliance be blessed,’
Said old Koshoi, spreading his palms.
To the bearded men and elders,
The matter was well known.
Toltoy, the son of Bagysh,
Has her as his promised bride.
He has a grave claim already sealed.
He too is of Kyrgyz lineage,
This one too is of Kyrgyz lineage,
And both have enemies to confront.
‘He took Chachykei away,’ they will say;
The Zhediger people will have a claim against Semetey.
She has a betrothed in a known place;
There is talk of endless turmoil.
I do not begrudge my daughter,
But this could bring us to destruction.
When we give this Chachykei,
If the great mass of Zhediger
Surges down upon us with battle cries,
What shall we be able to do?
How shall our encampment remain settled?
This wretched matter has its conditions:
Toltoy of the Zhediger
Has an oath of betrothal.
We have needlessly fallen into torment;
How are we to escape his oath?’
While Shaatemir was saying this,
Temir Khan grew wrathful,
And now his fury seized him.
The people watching
Had not the slightest strength remaining.
‘Your father's grave, you Bukharans!
Your elders with beards white as swans—
I shall utterly slaughter all of you.
I shall dig your pit deep,
And boil up your misery.
Before your very eyes,
I shall show marvels no people have seen!
Over this Bukhara here,
My seven forefathers were khans,
Ruling the people with justice.
When did I wrong you, Bukharans,
Even in the matter of your piebald colt?
This time I will not consent
To the way you drag things out.
Not merely one girl—Semetey
Let him take eighty girls, here they are!
Let him take all the people of Bukhara.
If Semetey wants,
Let him cut my beard and take me too.
Let him take all four kinds of livestock,
Let him take Bukhara's golden throne.
If he wishes, let him take old me!
From this orphan standing here,
I would not withhold my very life.
Saying, “They give away a betrothed girl,”
If Toltoy grows angry,
I have an answer ready to meet him,
And an army ready to contend with him.
If he comes out to a lance fight, I shall face him;
I shall answer him myself.
The obligation and the trouble
I shall meet in advance.
If the Zhediger babble,
I shall bring a thorough slaughter.
Whatever torment comes from it,
I shall meet it myself.’
The thousand strongmen of the royal treasury
Were given the command.
Semetey and Chachykei
To the gated fortress,
To Temir Khan's royal court,
They brought them there.
Slaughtering ninety fat mares,
Slaughtering ninety milk-fed camel calves,
Heaping up clarified butter,
Filling the place with wealth,
Spreading food and drink everywhere,
Staging festivities no one could devise,
Ninety from each of four kinds,
He had each kind of livestock slaughtered.
Every wandering dervish and pauper
He fed for ninety days in succession.
He launched great festivities,
With fat lambs and tender heads,
He had them boiled vigorously until done.
Merriment brought the dawn,
And laughter saw the sun set.
In those days in Bukhara,
He had the dutars played,
And about sixty of his Sarts
He had them all sing songs.
He had the booming drums struck,
And those who performed these dances,
The women dancers, he had brought,
Increasing the entertainment.
They slaughtered a calf for the rite,
And had the kok-boru contest played.
Entering the kok-boru,
The strongmen swaggered about,
And the khojas bustled grandly.
Gripping their whips between their teeth,
Each urged on his lone horse.
They made wondrous entertainments,
And great feats no one had seen:
Bald men butted heads with one another.
To the bald man who won the butting,
They granted what he asked,
From the treasury's single-humped camels,
Catching nine and giving them to him.
With festivities no one had known,
They held a feast for nine days.
Of the white-turbaned khojas,
And the lesson-reading mullahs,
They gathered the learned men.
It was Bukhara's custom:
They recited the khutba and solemnized the marriage.
At that time Semetey
Took a wife and established a household.
He became a khan like his father,
A man of surpassing honor.
Your orphan, son of the gray-maned hero,
Prepared to move to Talas,
To go to where his father Manas had lived.
Manas's orphan son—
His coming departure was plain to see.
Bukhara, which had raised him,
Shed tears from its eyes.
Its ruler Temir Khan wept,
And Ysmayyl wept as well.
Then the people of Bukhara wept together.
All those who wept
Wept in sorrow for themselves.
‘If he were Bukhara's protector,
This dear orphan of ours,
No calamity would befall us,’ they wept.
In the city of broad Bukhara,
Treasure filled eight buildings:
Red gold coins and rubies,
Mixed with costly goods.
